Chapter 4: Render Tags

Open in VS Code

So far every result has been a table. Malloy's renderer can also draw bar charts, line charts, dashboards, and big-number KPI cards. It can also format numbers as currency, percentages, or "12.3k." You ask for all of this with render tags: short lines that start with # and sit right above a query or a field.

From this chapter on, any result in the book can be a chart.

import "names.malloy"
import "ecommerce.malloy"

How tags work

A tag is a line beginning with # (a hash and a space). It attaches to whatever comes directly after it:

  • above run:, it applies to the whole result

  • above a field (aggregate:, group_by:, or a single field name), it applies to that column

  • above nest:, it applies to that nested result

Tags don't change what data comes back. They only change how it's drawn.

⚠️ # is not a comment. In Malloy, comments start with // or --. A line that starts with # is a tag. A misspelled tag is quietly ignored.

📘 Malloy docs. Visualizations overview · Annotations and tags

Bar charts

# bar_chart draws the first group_by: field along the x-axis and the first measure as the bar height.

# bar_chart
run: names -> {
  group_by: state
  aggregate: total_births
  limit: 15
}

SELECT 
   base."state" as "state",
   COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0) as "total_births"
FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 desc NULLS LAST
LIMIT 15

Add a second group_by: and the bars split into colored series. Here each decade gets a bar for girls and one for boys:

# bar_chart
run: names -> {
  where: decade >= 1950
  group_by: decade, gender
  aggregate: total_births
  order_by: decade
}

    "total_births": "2623185"

SELECT 
   (FLOOR(base."year"*1.0/10))*10 as "decade",
   base."gender" as "gender",
   COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0) as "total_births"
FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
WHERE ((FLOOR(base."year"*1.0/10))*10)>=1950
GROUP BY 1,2
ORDER BY 1 ASC NULLS LAST

Line charts

# line_chart is the natural choice for trends. Put a time (or a year) first in group_by:. How popular were three classic names over time?

# line_chart
run: names -> {
  where: name = 'Mary' | 'Linda' | 'Emma', gender = 'F'
  group_by: year_born, name
  aggregate: total_births
  order_by: year_born

SELECT 
   base."year" as "year_born",
   base."name" as "name",
   COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0) as "total_births"
FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
WHERE (base."name" IN ('Mary','Linda','Emma'))
AND (base."gender"='F')
GROUP BY 1,2
ORDER BY 1 ASC NULLS LAST

Again, the second group_by: (name) became the series, so each name gets its own line. Linda had one enormous spike after World War II. Emma came back in the 2000s.

SELECT 
   DATE_TRUNC('month', base."created_at") as "order_month",
   COALESCE(SUM(base."sale_price"),0) as "total_sales",
   base."status" as "status"
FROM 'data/order_items.parquet' as base
GROUP BY 1,3
ORDER BY 1 ASC NULLS LAST

📘 Malloy docs. Line charts

Charts inside nests

Tags work on nest: too. This puts a small chart inside every row, which is one of Malloy's best tricks. For each of the 5 most popular girls' names of all time, show its trend line:

run: names -> {
  where: gender = 'F'
  group_by: name
  aggregate: total_births
  # line_chart
  nest: trend is {
    group_by: year_born
    aggregate: total_births
    order_by: year_born
  }
  limit: 5
}

WITH __stage0 AS (
  SELECT
    group_set,
    base."name" as "name__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      base."year"
      END as "year_born__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__1"
  FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
  CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(GENERATE_SERIES(0,1,1)) as group_set  ) as group_set
  WHERE base."gender"='F'
  GROUP BY 1,2,4
)
, __stage1 AS (
  SELECT
    *,
   CASE WHEN GROUP_SET=0 THEN
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_set ORDER BY  "total_births__0" desc) END  as __row_number__0 
  FROM __stage0
)
, __stage2 AS (
  SELECT
    *,
    MAX(CASE WHEN group_set IN (0,1) THEN CASE WHEN (GROUP_SET = 0 AND __row_number__0 > 5) THEN 1 ELSE 0 END
                 END) OVER(PARTITION BY CAST("name__0" as VARCHAR)) as __shaving__0 
  FROM __stage1 WHERE 1=1
)
, __stage3 AS (
  SELECT *
  FROM __stage2
  WHERE NOT ((group_set IN (0,1) AND __shaving__0 > 0)
  )
)
SELECT
  "name__0" as "name",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "total_births__0" END) as "total_births",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "year_born": "year_born__1", 
    "total_births": "total_births__1"}  ORDER BY  "year_born__1" ASC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=1),[]) as "trend"
FROM __stage3
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 desc NULLS LAST
LIMIT 5

Number formatting

Raw numbers like 0.0734 or 4744743.4469 are hard to read. Tags on a field fix that:

Tag Example output
# percent 7.34%
# currency $4,744,743.45
# number="#,##0.0" 4,744,743.4
# number=1k 4,745k
# number=1m 4.74m
# number=auto picks k, m, or b for you
# label="Total Sales" changes the column heading 
run: order_items -> {
  group_by: order_year is created_at.year
  aggregate:
    # label="Revenue"
    # currency
    revenue is sale_price.sum()

    # number=1k
    items_sold_k is count()

    # percent
    share_of_revenue is sale_price.sum() / all(sale_price.sum())
  order_by: order_year
}
QUERY RESULTS 
[
  {
    "order_year": "2019-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    "revenue": 1318595.5448319912,
    "items_sold_k": 28574,
    "share_of_revenue": 0.10493114858125521
  },
  {
    "order_year": "2020-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    "revenue": 2602043.069360018,
    "items_sold_k": 56022,
    "share_of_revenue": 0.20706528927384643
  },
  {
    "order_year": "2021-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    "revenue": 3900910.8143820763,
    "items_sold_k": 84149,
    "share_of_revenue": 0.3104265397152584
  },
  {
    "order_year": "2022-01-01T00:00:00.000Z",
    "revenue": 4744743.446900487,
    "items_sold_k": 102274,
    "share_of_revenue": 0.3775770224296399
  }
]
WITH __stage0 AS (
  SELECT
    group_set,
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      DATE_TRUNC('year', base."created_at")
      END as "order_year__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."sale_price"),0)
      END as "revenue__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COUNT(1)
      END as "items_sold_k__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."sale_price"),0)
      END*1.0/MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."sale_price"),0)
      END) OVER () as "share_of_revenue__1"
  FROM 'data/order_items.parquet' as base
  CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(GENERATE_SERIES(0,1,1)) as group_set  ) as group_set
  GROUP BY 1,2
)
SELECT
  "order_year__1" as "order_year",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN "revenue__1" END) as "revenue",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN "items_sold_k__1" END) as "items_sold_k",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN "share_of_revenue__1" END) as "share_of_revenue"
FROM __stage0
WHERE group_set NOT IN (0)
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 1 ASC NULLS LAST

(all() gives the grand total across all rows. You'll learn it properly in Chapter 11.)

Put format tags in the model, and every query that uses the field gets the formatting for free. In ecommerce.malloy, total_sales is defined like this:

measure:
  # currency
  total_sales is sale_price.sum()

That's why total_sales has shown up as dollars in every chapter.

📘 Malloy docs. Number formatting

Big values (KPI cards)

# big_value shows each measure as a large number. It's great for the top of a report.

# big_value
run: order_items -> {
  where: created_at.year = @2022
  aggregate:
    # label="2022 Revenue"
    total_sales
    # label="Orders"
    order_count
    # label="Avg Item Price"
    avg_sale_price
}
QUERY RESULTS 
[
  {
    "total_sales": 4744743.446900487,
    "order_count": 99785,
    "avg_sale_price": 46.3924697078484
  }
]
SELECT 
   COALESCE(SUM(base."sale_price"),0) as "total_sales",
   count(distinct base."order_id") as "order_count",
   AVG(base."sale_price") as "avg_sale_price"
FROM 'data/order_items.parquet' as base
WHERE (DATE_TRUNC('year', base."created_at")>=TIMESTAMP '2022-01-01 00:00:00') and (DATE_TRUNC('year', base."created_at")<TIMESTAMP '2023-01-01 00:00:00')

📘 Malloy docs. Big values

Dashboards

# dashboard lays a nested query out as tiles instead of a table. Each top-level measure becomes a KPI card, and each nest becomes a panel that can carry its own chart tag. # break starts a new row of tiles.

# dashboard
run: names -> {
  where: state = 'CA'
  aggregate:
    total_births
    name_count
  # line_chart
  nest: births_by_year is {
    group_by: year_born
    aggregate: total_births
    order_by: year_born
  }
  # bar_chart
  nest: by_gender is {
    group_by: gender
    aggregate: total_births
  }
  # break
  nest: top_girls is by_name + { where: gender = 'F', limit: 5 }
  nest: top_boys is by_name + { where: gender = 'M', limit: 5 }
}

WITH __stage0 AS (
  SELECT
    group_set,
    CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
      count(distinct base."name")
      END as "name_count__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      base."year"
      END as "year_born__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=2 THEN
      base."gender"
      END as "gender__2",
    CASE WHEN group_set=2 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__2",
    CASE WHEN group_set=3 THEN
      base."name"
      END as "name__3",
    CASE WHEN group_set=3 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__3",
    CASE WHEN group_set=4 THEN
      base."name"
      END as "name__4",
    CASE WHEN group_set=4 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__4"
  FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
  CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(GENERATE_SERIES(0,4,1)) as group_set  ) as group_set
  WHERE (base."state"='CA')
  AND ((group_set NOT IN (3) OR (group_set IN (3) AND base."gender"='F')))
  AND ((group_set NOT IN (4) OR (group_set IN (4) AND base."gender"='M')))
  GROUP BY 1,4,6,8,10
)
, __stage1 AS (
  SELECT
    *,
   CASE WHEN GROUP_SET=3 THEN
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_set ORDER BY  "total_births__3" desc) END  as __row_number__3,
  CASE WHEN GROUP_SET=4 THEN
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY group_set ORDER BY  "total_births__4" desc) END  as __row_number__4 
  FROM __stage0
)
, __stage2 AS (
  SELECT * FROM __stage1
   WHERE  NOT ((GROUP_SET = 3 AND __row_number__3 > 5)
   OR (GROUP_SET = 4 AND __row_number__4 > 5))
)
SELECT
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "total_births__0" END) as "total_births",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "name_count__0" END) as "name_count",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "year_born": "year_born__1", 
    "total_births": "total_births__1"}  ORDER BY  "year_born__1" ASC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=1),[]) as "births_by_year",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "gender": "gender__2", 
    "total_births": "total_births__2"}  ORDER BY  "total_births__2" DESC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=2),[]) as "by_gender",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "name": "name__3", 
    "total_births": "total_births__3"}  ORDER BY  "total_births__3" DESC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=3),[]) as "top_girls",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "name": "name__4", 
    "total_births": "total_births__4"}  ORDER BY  "total_births__4" DESC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=4),[]) as "top_boys"
FROM __stage2

A dashboard with a group_by: at the top level makes one dashboard per group. Here's one for each of three states:

# dashboard
run: names -> {
  where: state = 'UT' | 'VT' | 'HI'
  group_by: state
  aggregate: total_births
  # bar_chart
  nest: by_decade is {
    group_by: decade
    aggregate: total_births
    order_by: decade
  }
  nest: top_names is by_name + { limit: 5 }
}

WITH __stage0 AS (
  SELECT
    group_set,
    base."state" as "state__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__0",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      (FLOOR(base."year"*1.0/10))*10
      END as "decade__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=1 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__1",
    CASE WHEN group_set=2 THEN
      base."name"
      END as "name__2",
    CASE WHEN group_set=2 THEN
      COALESCE(SUM(base."number"),0)
      END as "total_births__2"
  FROM 'data/usa_names.parquet' as base
  CROSS JOIN (SELECT UNNEST(GENERATE_SERIES(0,2,1)) as group_set  ) as group_set
  WHERE base."state" IN ('UT','VT','HI')
  GROUP BY 1,2,4,6
)
, __stage1 AS (
  SELECT
    *,
   CASE WHEN GROUP_SET=2 THEN
                 ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY CAST("state__0" as VARCHAR), group_set ORDER BY  "total_births__2" desc) END  as __row_number__2 
  FROM __stage0
)
, __stage2 AS (
  SELECT * FROM __stage1
   WHERE  NOT ((GROUP_SET = 2 AND __row_number__2 > 5))
)
SELECT
  "state__0" as "state",
  MAX(CASE WHEN group_set=0 THEN "total_births__0" END) as "total_births",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "decade": "decade__1", 
    "total_births": "total_births__1"}  ORDER BY  "decade__1" ASC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=1),[]) as "by_decade",
  COALESCE(LIST({
    "name": "name__2", 
    "total_births": "total_births__2"}  ORDER BY  "total_births__2" DESC NULLS LAST) FILTER (WHERE group_set=2),[]) as "top_names"
FROM __stage2
GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 desc NULLS LAST

📘 Malloy docs. Dashboards

A few more tags worth knowing

Tag What it does
# transpose swaps rows and columns
# hidden hides a field (handy for sort-only columns)
# list / # list_detail shows a nest as a compact comma-separated list
# shape_map colors a U.S. map by state (needs 2-letter state codes)
# scatter_chart x/y scatter plot

GROUP BY 1
ORDER BY 2 desc NULLS LAST

Key takeaways

  • A render tag is a # ... line above a query, field, or nest. It changes how results are drawn, not what they are.

  • # bar_chart and # line_chart use the first group_by: as the x-axis. A second group_by: becomes the series.

  • # dashboard turns nests into tiles. # big_value shows KPI cards.

  • Format numbers with # currency, # percent, # number=..., and rename columns with # label=.... Put formats in the model so they're always applied.

🎯 Challenge 4.1: Chart your name. Make a # line_chart of births per year for your name (or any name), with one line per gender.

🎯 Challenge 4.2: Bar chart of name lengths. Make a # bar_chart that shows total_births by name_length for babies born in 2021. Sort by name_length so the bars go from short to long names.

🎯 Challenge 4.3: Build a dashboard. Make a # dashboard for the e-commerce store for 2021. It should include: a # big_value-style row of measures at the top (total_sales, order_count), a # line_chart nest of sales by month, and a # bar_chart nest of the top 10 product categories (inventory_items.product_category) by sales.
